check.a: RPO concerns acceptable recent data loss; RTO concerns acceptable recovery duration.

check.q: Why keep a copy in another account?
check.a: It reduces the chance that one compromise or mistake destroys every copy.

check.q: What proves a backup is usable?
check.a: A successful restore with checked data and application behaviour.

chapters.title: Maintaining and Evolving the Application
chapters.question: How do you choose between new features, defects, updates, and a rising hosting bill?
chapters.summary: Maintenance keeps a live application useful, affordable, and safe as its circumstances change. Evidence-based priorities and regular upkeep prevent small neglected problems from turning into disruptive rewrites or emergencies.

sections.heading: Collect evidence in one place
paragraphs: Listen through support messages, a feedback link, and short conversations with active users. Compare requests with privacy-respecting usage information and operational evidence such as failures or slow journeys. A loud request may matter, but it is not automatically more important than an issue quietly preventing many people from finishing their work.

Record the evidence in one issue tracker rather than leaving decisions scattered across inboxes and memory. Distinguish a bug, an improvement, routine upkeep, and a capacity concern. Link reports that describe the same underlying problem. Clear records let you revisit why work was prioritised and help an assistant understand the actual outcome needed instead of implementing the most recent suggestion literally.

sections.heading: Prioritise impact and effort
paragraphs: Estimate impact on users and the product alongside effort, uncertainty, and risk. High-impact work with modest effort is often worth doing soon. High-impact, high-effort work needs planning and smaller increments. Low-impact quick changes can be batched, while low-impact expensive work may not deserve a place on the roadmap.

Security vulnerabilities and bugs that expose or lose data jump this ordinary queue. Assess them promptly even if the implementation effort is uncomfortable. Reconnect priorities with the original product goals: an interesting rewrite does not necessarily help the people the application exists to serve. Use estimates as discussion tools, not precise mathematical truth, and update them when new evidence changes what you know.

sections.heading: Reserve regular time for code health
paragraphs: Apply small dependency updates regularly, reviewing release notes carefully for major versions and handling security fixes promptly. Automated proposals can reduce the effort of noticing available updates, but tests and human review still decide whether a change is safe. Avoid accumulating years of version jumps into one difficult migration.

Track technical debt: known shortcuts or weaknesses that make future changes harder. Reserve a recurring share of maintenance time for paying down the most costly items, especially in frequently changed areas. Give each bug fix a regression test. Investigate flaky checks and repair or deliberately replace them instead of allowing random failures to become normal background noise.

sections.heading: Keep documentation connected to reality
paragraphs: A repository’s README, design notes, decision records, runbook, and agent instructions are working tools. Review them after significant changes so setup steps, operational procedures, and architectural assumptions remain true. Outdated instructions can cause the same mistake repeatedly, whether the next person following them is you, a colleague, or an AI agent.

Keep maintenance work visible beside feature development. A short routine is easier to sustain than an occasional heroic cleanup. For example, review issues weekly, update proposals on a fixed weekday, and set aside a monthly session for debt, documentation, costs, and capacity. Give these tasks an owner and a checkable result so they do not remain permanently optional.

sections.heading: Watch money and resource limits
paragraphs: Review cloud bills monthly and set budget alerts. Find the services and features driving spend: database tiers, storage, log retention, network traffic, and paid API calls can all grow quietly. A temporary upgrade during an incident may remain expensive long after the emergency ends. Cost visibility belongs in engineering decisions even for a solo project.

Watch database size, connection use, and response times alongside spending. Do not downgrade a service blindly just to reduce the next bill; first check whether its capacity is still needed. Equally, do not scale infrastructure to conceal an inefficient query without understanding it. Follow evidence from a cost or performance symptom to its cause, then verify that the improvement preserves user experience.

sections.heading: Revisit architecture when assumptions change
paragraphs: An architectural decision record, or ADR, explains a choice and the conditions under which it should be reconsidered. As usage and requirements change, compare new evidence with those revisit conditions. A need for richer search, for example, should trigger a deliberate evaluation rather than an unannounced switch of databases during an unrelated feature.

Changing a past decision does not mean it was foolish when made. The right structure for a small launch can differ from the right structure for a mature product. Record the new trade-offs and migrate in small checked increments. Resist an assistant’s tendency to recommend a new framework or wholesale rewrite before establishing the actual problem. Continued simplicity comes from deliberate upkeep, not from avoiding change or chasing every new tool.

chapters.keyIdea: Treat updates, debt, documentation, costs, and capacity as recurring product work guided by evidence.
chapters.taskboard: Taskboard’s routine combines weekly issue triage and dependency review with monthly upkeep and cost checks. Quarterly reviews compare architectural assumptions with current needs, including the decision-record trigger for richer task search.

walkthrough.title: Investigate a growing hosting bill
steps: Break the bill down by service and compare it with previous months.
Check whether an incident-time database upgrade and verbose logging were left in place.
Adjust the tier only after reviewing capacity, and set appropriate log levels and retention.
Add a budget alert and a runbook reminder to revisit temporary emergency settings.

mistakes: Adding features indefinitely while security updates and debt accumulate.
Ignoring cost and capacity until they become an emergency.
Replacing the application wholesale instead of improving the troublesome parts incrementally.
aiMistakes: An agent may recommend a rewrite without evidence: ask which measured problem it solves.
It may upgrade every major dependency together: split and verify the changes.
It may add paid API calls to each request: inspect usage paths and estimate cost before release.
tryIt: Build a board containing bugs, improvements, upkeep, and costs; prioritise each item.
Schedule a monthly maintenance block and identify one architecture revisit condition.

check.q: Which issues override the ordinary impact–effort ranking?
check.a: Security problems and defects that lose or expose data.

check.q: Why review costs regularly?
check.a: Quiet growth and forgotten temporary settings can create avoidable expense.

check.q: When should an architectural decision be revisited?
check.a: When changed requirements or evidence meet its documented reconsideration conditions.
